title: Linked List Cycle
description:
Given the head of a linked list, determine whether the list contains a cycle.

A cycle exists when some node can be reached again by repeatedly following next. The input describes the list as {"values": [...], "pos": i}, where pos is the index of the node the last node points back to, or -1 when the list ends normally. pos is not passed to your function — it only describes how the list is wired before you receive it.

Return true if there is a cycle and false otherwise.

Constraints:

  • The list holds between 0 and 10^4 nodes.
  • -10^5 <= Node.val <= 10^5.
  • pos is -1 or a valid index in the list.
  • Solving this with O(1) extra memory is the point of the exercise; a set of visited nodes works but uses O(n).

exampleTestCases.explanation: The tail links back to index 1, so following next never reaches an end.
Two nodes pointing at each other form the smallest two-node cycle.
A single node whose next is None terminates, so there is no cycle.

testCases.explanation: The tail links back to index 1, so following next never reaches an end.
Two nodes pointing at each other form the smallest two-node cycle.
A single node whose next is None terminates, so there is no cycle.
An empty list has nothing to loop through.
A node pointing at itself is a cycle of length one, which a fast pointer must still catch.
A plain five node list ends normally.
The tail pointing at itself is a cycle, even though only one node repeats.
The tail links back to the head, so the whole list is one loop.
Repeated values must not be mistaken for a repeated node; identity is what matters.
Negative values change nothing about the traversal.
